questions.solution_html:

questions.question: Explain the importance of Archegoniates in plant evolution.
questions.solution_html:
• ● Evolutionary link in the transition of plants from aquatic to terrestrial environments, showing 1
  • e
  • adaptations such as a protected embryo and specialized reproductive organs. g
  • a
  • P
  • ● The presence of the archegonium, a multicellular female sex organ enclosing the egg- protecting
  • gametes and the developing zygote from desiccation.
  • ● Retention of the fertilized egg (zygote) within the archegonium, where it developed into a multicellular

questions.question: Give an account of three subclasses of class Bryopsida as per Rothmaler's classification.
questions.solution_html:
• Give an account of three subclasses of class Bryopsida as per Rothmaler's classification.
  • ○ Sphagnidae (Peat Mosses)-Primitive group including peat mosses.Possess branched gametophytes
  • with clusters of branches at nodes. Sporophyte lacks peristome; capsule opens by an explosive lid
  • mechanism. Example: Sphagnum.
  • ○ Andreaeidae (Granite Mosses)-Small group found mostly in cold and alpine regions.Capsules open by
  • longitudinal slits instead of an operculum (lantern mosses). Spores are released gradually; peristome
  • is absent. Example: Andreaea.
  • ○ Bryidae (True Mosses)-The largest and most advanced subclass. Possess a well-differentiated stem
  • and leafy gametophyte. Sporophyte has a complex peristome with two rings of teeth (diplolepidous).
  • Example: Funaria, Polytrichum
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the morphology of Polysiphonia.
questions.solution_html:
• Marine, filamentous, branched thallus that appears as delicate, feathery tufts. Reddish-brown to dark red in
  • color and grows attached to rocks, other alga by holdfast. The plant is differentiated into a holdfast
  • (attachment structure), main axis, and lateral branches. Polysiphonous structure – Central axial cell
  • surrounded by pericentral cells. Regular, alternate or spiral branching; presence of trichoblasts. Cells
  • contain Pit connections, discoid chloroplasts, cellulose wall. Lack pyrenoids. Reproductive structures
  • (spermatangia, carpogonia, cystocarps, and tetrasporangia) develop on special branches. (5 points with
  • description)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the vegetative features of gymnosperms with suitable examples.
questions.solution_html:
• The main plant body is the diploid sporophyte, which is differentiated into true roots, stem, and leaves.
  • ○ well-developed tap root system. Roots often form mycorrhizal associations (e.g., Pinus) or coralloid
  • roots housing cyanobacteria for nitrogen fixation (Cycas).
  • ○ Stems are erect, woody, and branched (Pinus) or unbranched (Cycas). They show secondary growth
  • due to vascular cambium, forming annual rings like in dicots. Branched or unbranched. Leaf Scars
  • due to the shedding of old leaves.
  • ○ Vascular Tissue: The wood (secondary xylem) generally consists of tracheids but lacks vessels (except
  • in Gnetophytes like Gnetum). The secondary wood is classified as: Manoxylic Wood (e.g., Cycas) and
  • Pycnoxylic Wood (e.g., Pinus). 2
  • e
  • ○ Dimorphism in leaves: two types of leaves. Scale Leaves and Foliage Leavess g
  • a
  • P
  • ○ Xerophytic Adaptations of leaves: Needle or Scale-like Shape,Thick Cuticle, Sunken Stomata
  • Transfusion Tissue ( Any 5 features with explanation and examples)
questions.final_answer: Transfusion Tissue ( Any 5 features with explanation and examples)

questions.question: Distinguish between vegetative cells and reproductive cells in Oedogonium.
questions.solution_html:
• Vegetative Cells Reproductive Cells
  • Shape Cylindrical, uniform diameter Zoosporangia: slightly swollen; Oogonia
  • distinctly swollen; Antheridia: smaller, box
  • like
  • Size Normal, elongated Oogonia much larger; Antheridia smaller
  • Function Photosynthesis, growth Reproduction - spore/gamete production
  • Contents Single reticulate chloroplast, Zoospores with multiple flagella; egg or sperms
  • nucleus
  • Cap cells present Oogonia develop pores; zoosporangia rupture
questions.final_answer: Cap cells present Oogonia develop pores; zoosporangia rupture

questions.question: Write any five distinguishing characters of Puccinia.
questions.solution_html:
• Obligate Parasitism. Polymorphism - producing up to five distinct types of spores- (Pycniospores
  • (Spermatia), Aeciospores, Uredospores, Teliospores, Basidiospores. Heteroecious life cycle-require two
  • different host plants. Dikaryotic Phase Dominance: specifically the Uredial stage on the primary host
  • responsible for the rapid, repeating spread of the disease. The presence of the characteristic Teliospore (or
  • Teleutospore) - two-celled, thick-walled, stalked spore where karyogamy (nuclear fusion) occurs, and it
  • functions primarily as a resting or overwintering spore. Rust fungi- Major agricultural pathogen requiring
  • disease management strategies (5 points with explanation)
questions.final_answer: disease management strategies (5 points with explanation)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Analyze the significance of antheridia and archegonia in Riccia
questions.solution_html:
• Analyze the significance of antheridia and archegonia in Riccia
  • - Sites of Gamete Formation
  • - Protection of Gametes-Both organs are multicellular and jacketed, providing protection to gametes
  • from desiccation and mechanical injury in terrestrial habitat.
  • - Facilitation of Fertilization
  • - Site of Zygote Formation- Fertilization occurs within the archegonium
  • - Initiation of Sporophytic Generation-The zygote develops into the sporophyte while still attached
  • to the gametophyte.This marks the transition from gametophytic to sporophytic phase, ensuring
  • alternation of generations.( Liberal valuation)
